verses.bibleText: I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The word 'therefore' turns the saving truths of chapters 1–3 into a summons for daily life. God has chosen His people in Christ, redeemed them by His blood, raised them from spiritual death, reconciled Jew and Gentile in one body, and made them His dwelling through the Spirit. Christian conduct is the response to those mercies. It neither purchases salvation nor adds merit to Christ's finished work.

Paul appeals as 'the prisoner of the Lord.' His chains resulted from faithfulness to the Gentile mission entrusted to him, yet he does not describe himself as Rome's prisoner. His life, circumstances, and suffering belong to Christ. The costly setting gives moral weight to his appeal: the unity he seeks is not a comfortable ideal but part of the gospel for which he is willing to suffer.

The 'vocation' is not restricted to ordained ministry. Every believer has been called from alienation into fellowship with God and His people. To walk worthily is to let outward conduct correspond to that new identity. Grace establishes the relationship; obedience expresses it. The balance must be preserved. A holy life cannot earn the calling, but a life persistently opposed to the calling contradicts the confession that one has received it.

Paul begins the practical half of the letter with the church's unity rather than private religious achievement. A worthy walk is immediately visible in the way believers treat one another. The God who has created one new humanity in Christ expects that reconciliation to take concrete form in humility, patience, truthfulness, generosity, forgiveness, and love.

wordNotes.explanation: To walk describes the whole pattern of life. Worthily means in a manner corresponding to the calling received, not conduct that earns that calling.
The word means calling. Here it refers to God's gracious summons into salvation, holiness, hope, and membership in His reconciled people.

verses.bibleText: With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The worthy walk takes shape through qualities that preserve relationships. Humility comes first because pride continually fragments the church. In a society ordered by rank, honor, and competition, lowliness could be dismissed as weakness. The gospel gives it a new center in Christ, who possessed divine glory yet humbled Himself for the salvation of others. Christian humility recognizes every gift as received, every person as created by God, and every believer as a fellow member of Christ's body.

Meekness is the gentleness that refuses to use strength for self-assertion. It does not mean moral indecision or unwillingness to confront evil. Jesus was meek, yet He spoke with authority and opposed hypocrisy. Gentleness governs how truth is carried: without contempt, revenge, or delight in humiliating another.

Longsuffering is patience extended over time, especially when another person's weakness is costly. It restrains the impulse to retaliate, abandon, or condemn too quickly. Forbearing one another goes beyond passive tolerance. Believers carry the strain created by differences and imperfections because love seeks the other's ultimate good.

Such forbearance does not require concealing abuse, treating destructive behavior as harmless, or refusing proper correction. Love can establish boundaries and call sin by its name. Its distinguishing spirit is redemptive rather than vindictive. The church's unity depends less upon finding people who never irritate one another than upon receiving from Christ the humility and patience needed to love real people. These graces are not decorative virtues; they are the practical conditions in which the one body can live.

wordNotes.explanation: Humility is a truthful, God-centered estimate of oneself that rejects self-exaltation and willingly honors others. It is not self-hatred or denial of God-given worth.
The participle means bearing with or patiently putting up with one another. It describes sustained love amid real differences, weaknesses, and provocations.

verses.bibleText: Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The unity believers are to keep is 'the unity of the Spirit.' It originates in the Holy Spirit, not in human diplomacy. Through Christ's cross, God has reconciled formerly divided peoples in one body and given them access to the Father by one Spirit. The church therefore does not create its deepest unity; it receives it as part of salvation.

What God creates must nevertheless be guarded. The command to endeavour indicates energetic, continuing attention. Spiritual unity can be obscured by pride, racial or social prejudice, personal rivalry, careless speech, doctrinal manipulation, and refusal to forgive. Believers cannot preserve it merely by affirming unity in principle while nourishing attitudes that tear relationships apart.

Peace is the bond that holds the body together. In Ephesians, peace is more than the absence of argument. Christ Himself is the church's peace because His death has removed hostility and reconciled both Jew and Gentile to God. Maintaining peace therefore means living consistently with the cross—renouncing superiority, seeking reconciliation, and treating fellow believers as members of the same redeemed humanity.

Unity is not uniformity. The following verses will celebrate different gifts and ministries. Nor is unity obtained by surrendering revealed truth, since the church must later reach the unity of the faith and resist every wind of false doctrine. Biblical peace joins truth with love. It refuses both divisive pride and superficial agreement. The Spirit-created unity of the church becomes visible when believers pursue reconciliation without sacrificing fidelity to Christ.

wordNotes.explanation: The word conveys eagerness, diligence, and sustained effort. Preserving unity is an active responsibility rather than a passive wish.

wordNotes.term: bond of peace — σύνδεσμος τῆς εἰρήνης (syndesmos tēs eirēnēs)
wordNotes.explanation: A syndesmos is a bond, fastener, or ligament. Peace functions as the binding relationship that holds the members of Christ's body together.

verses.bibleText: There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul grounds the call to unity in realities that believers already share. There is one body because Christ did not create separate covenant peoples for different ethnic or social groups. Through His death He reconciled Jew and Gentile to God in one body. Local congregations may differ in language, culture, organization, and maturity, but all who truly belong to Christ are members of the same spiritual organism.

The body is one because the Spirit is one. The Holy Spirit does not promote competing loyalties or contradictory gospels. He gives life to every believer, incorporates them into Christ's body, dwells within the church, and produces the character needed for fellowship. Genuine work of the Spirit therefore leads toward Christ-centered unity, holiness, and truth rather than personality cults or spiritual superiority.

The one hope corresponds to the one calling. Formerly the Gentile believers were without hope and without God in the world. Now they share the promised inheritance with all the saints. Their hope is not divided according to ancestry or status. Together they await Christ's appearing, the resurrection of the dead, the transformation of the living faithful, freedom from corruption, and the renewal of creation.

This shared hope gives unity an eternal horizon. Present disagreements must be viewed in light of the future in which God's redeemed people will live together in His kingdom. The final inheritance is not competing private rewards enjoyed through an innately immortal existence; it is the corporate fulfillment of God's promise when Christ raises His people and brings them into the life of the world to come. Those called to one future should begin learning the life of that future now.

wordNotes.explanation: Christian hope is confident expectation grounded in God's promise. It includes the completion of redemption, resurrection, the inheritance of the saints, and life in God's restored creation.

verses.bibleText: One Lord, one faith, one baptism,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The confession 'one Lord' places Jesus Christ at the center of Christian unity. In the Roman world many authorities claimed lordship, and religious life recognized many gods and lords. The church confesses that final authority belongs to Jesus alone. The wording also echoes Israel's confession that the Lord is one. By including Jesus within this confession, Paul speaks consistently with the full divine identity of the Son. Christ is not one religious master among others but the exalted Lord before whom every competing power must bow.

The one faith is the common trust placed in this Lord and the shared gospel through which He is known. Personal faith is not identical in strength or maturity among all believers, but its object and foundation are one. The church is not united by vague spirituality. It is united by the apostolic truth concerning the incarnate Son, His atoning death, bodily resurrection, exaltation, saving grace, and coming kingdom.

One baptism visibly marks entrance into this Christ-centered community. Baptism by water identifies the believer with Christ's death and resurrection and publicly confesses the end of the old allegiance. Its meaning cannot be separated from repentance, faith, and the transforming work of the Spirit. Water does not mechanically regenerate an unbelieving heart, nor does the ceremony earn acceptance with God. It is the appointed sign of union with Christ and incorporation into His people.

Because there is one baptism, no social class or ethnic group receives a superior initiation. All come to Christ as sinners dependent upon grace. The same burial with Christ and the same call to newness of life apply to each. The verse therefore joins doctrine, worship, and ethics: one Lord commands undivided loyalty, one faith excludes another gospel, and one baptism summons the whole church to live as the one new humanity it publicly professes to be.

wordNotes.explanation: The confession identifies Jesus Christ as the one sovereign Lord. The title echoes Old Testament language for the Lord God and excludes every rival claim to ultimate allegiance.

Baptism is the common Christian initiation that publicly identifies believers with Christ's death and resurrection and with His one body. The outward act bears witness to the inward reality received through faith and the Spirit.

verses.bibleText: One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The sevenfold confession of oneness reaches its climax in 'one God and Father.' The Spirit, the Lord Jesus, and the Father have each been named. Their distinct personal activity does not divide the divine work. The one God creates, redeems, calls, indwells, and directs one people toward one purpose.

God is Father in a special covenantal sense to those adopted through Jesus Christ. The statement should not be turned into universal salvation or the idea that every spiritual path relates humanity to God in the same way. Ephesians has already distinguished those alienated from God from those brought near by Christ's blood. Access to the Father comes through the Son in the Spirit.

The Father is 'above all' as sovereign ruler. No emperor, spiritual power, institution, or human leader can claim His place. He works 'through all,' accomplishing His purposes through the varied members of Christ's body. He is 'in you all,' dwelling within His reconciled people by the Spirit. Divine indwelling does not dissolve the distinction between Creator and creature. It means that God's presence animates and sanctifies the community He has made His temple.

The universal sovereignty of the Father gives Christian unity cosmic importance. God purposes to gather all things in Christ, and the church is the present demonstration of that reconciling purpose. Division rooted in pride, prejudice, or rivalry contradicts the character of the family whose Father is one. Believers do not achieve oneness by denying legitimate differences; they manifest the unity already established by the one Father who rules them, works through them, and lives among them.

wordNotes.term: above all, and through all, and in you all — ἐπὶ πάντων καὶ διὰ πάντων καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν (epi pantōn kai dia pantōn kai en pasin)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrases proclaim the Father's sovereignty, active working, and indwelling presence. In context they especially describe His relation to the united community of believers while also fitting His universal rule as Creator.

verses.bibleText: But unto every one of us is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The repeated word 'one' now gives way to 'every one.' Unity does not erase individuality. Christ gives distinct grace to each member so that the one body may function through a rich diversity of service. The contrast guards the church from two errors: fragmentation that treats gifts as private possessions, and uniformity that expects every believer to serve in the same way.

Grace here is not limited to the saving favor by which sinners are accepted, although every ministry gift rests upon that grace. It includes the role Christ assigns and the power needed to fulfill it. Paul had earlier described his own commission to preach among the Gentiles as grace given to him. What was uniquely apostolic in his vocation does not cancel the broader principle: every believer receives some capacity for the good of the body.

Christ determines the measure. Gifts therefore provide no basis for boasting, envy, or discouragement. A public ministry is not necessarily more valuable than quiet service, and a highly visible ability does not make its possessor more loved by God. The measure belongs to Christ's wisdom, while faithfulness belongs to the recipient's responsibility.

No member is spiritually unnecessary. Each has received grace, and each is called to contribute. Gifts become distorted when used to create dependence upon a personality, secure status, or compete for recognition. Their purpose appears in the verses that follow: equipping the saints, building Christ's body, protecting it from deception, and helping it grow in love. Diversity becomes a servant of unity when every gift remains under the authority of the Giver.

wordNotes.explanation: Here grace includes a ministry assignment and the divine enablement needed to carry it out. It remains an undeserved gift rather than a mark of personal superiority.

wordNotes.term: according to the measure — κατὰ τὸ μέτρον (kata to metron)
wordNotes.explanation: Christ apportions each gift according to His wise measure. Different measures describe diverse functions, not differing degrees of value before God.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore he saith, When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul supports Christ's distribution of grace by drawing upon Psalm 68. The psalm celebrates God as the victorious divine Warrior who scatters His enemies, ascends in triumph, and strengthens His people. Paul presents that movement in a Christ-centered form: the risen Lord ascends on high, leads captivity captive, and gives gifts to humanity.

The wording in Ephesians emphasizes giving, whereas the Hebrew and Greek forms of the psalm speak of receiving gifts. The apostle is not overturning the psalm's message. A victorious king received tribute and then distributed the spoils of victory among his people. Paul brings that implied distribution to the foreground because his concern is the grace Christ gives to the church.

'Captivity' is best understood within the imagery of conquest. Sin, death, hostile spiritual powers, and every force opposed to God's reign have met their conqueror in the crucified and risen Christ. The verse need not be interpreted as a procession of conscious souls released from an underworld prison. Its emphasis is the public triumph of the ascended Lord over the powers that had enslaved humanity.

Christ's gifts are therefore the fruit of victory. Apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, teachers, and the varied graces given to all believers are not emergency measures supplied by a defeated or absent leader. They come from the enthroned Christ whose authority reaches above every hostile power. Ministry is possible because the decisive battle has been won.

The victor does not hoard the spoils. He equips His people. His conquest creates a serving community rather than an elite class of conquerors. Every gift used to proclaim truth, reconcile believers, care for the weak, and build the church is evidence that the risen Christ reigns and shares the benefits of His triumph.

wordNotes.term: led captivity captive — ᾐχμαλώτευσεν αἰχμαλωσίαν (ēchmalōteusen aichmalōsian)
wordNotes.explanation: The expression pictures a victorious ruler leading a captured host in triumph. Applied to Christ, it proclaims His decisive conquest of the powers that held humanity in bondage.

verses.bibleText: (Now that he ascended, what is it but that he also descended first into the lower parts of the earth?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Christ's ascent implies a prior descent. The KJV makes the sequence explicit with the word 'first'; some ancient manuscripts omit that adverb, but the contrast between humiliation and exaltation remains. The One who rose to the highest place had entered the lowest condition.

The phrase 'the lower parts of the earth' has been understood in two principal ways. It may describe the earth as the lower realm in contrast with heaven, so that the descent embraces the incarnation: the eternal Son came from heavenly glory into genuine human life. It may more specifically describe the depths associated with death and burial. The second reading fits expressions in the Psalms that associate the lower parts of the earth with the grave, while the first fits the familiar New Testament pattern of Christ descending from heaven and returning to the Father.

The two ideas need not be set sharply against each other. Christ's descent began with His self-humbling incarnation and reached its deepest point in His suffering, death, and burial. The Son truly entered mortal human existence and genuinely died. His humanity was not an appearance, and His death was not merely the release of an immortal spirit from a body.

The wording does not require the later idea that Christ preached a saving gospel to conscious dead souls or released Old Testament saints from a place called limbo. Scripture places the hope of the dead in resurrection. Christ entered the domain of death by dying, broke its power through His resurrection, and ascended as the living Lord. The grave could not hold Him.

Paul's main concern is not to map an unseen geography. He is showing the universal reach of Christ's victory. No depth of humiliation, death, or hostile power lies beyond His authority. The One who gives gifts to the church is the Son who came fully into humanity's condition, carried His saving mission through death, and emerged victorious. His exaltation therefore rests upon accomplished redemption, and His people can serve without fear of powers already placed beneath His feet.

wordNotes.term: the lower parts of the earth — τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς (ta katōtera merē tēs gēs)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase may mean the lower regions belonging to the earth, especially the grave or realm of death, or the lower region that is the earth, referring more broadly to Christ's incarnation. Both readings emphasize His profound humiliation before exaltation.

verses.bibleText: He that descended is the same also that ascended up far above all heavens, that he might fill all things.)

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The identity of the descending and ascending One is emphatic. The Jesus who entered human weakness, died, and was buried is the same Christ who rose bodily and ascended above every heaven. Exaltation does not discard His humanity. The incarnate Son remains the representative and brother of the redeemed even as He exercises universal lordship.

'Far above all heavens' announces supremacy rather than merely describing distance. Earlier Paul placed Christ above every principality, power, might, dominion, and name. No spiritual hierarchy, earthly empire, or cosmic force stands alongside Him as an equal. His ascension is enthronement.

From that exalted position Christ is not inactive. He ministers for His people, pours out the Spirit, governs His church, and distributes gifts. His once-for-all sacrifice requires no repetition, while His living heavenly ministry continually applies the benefits of that completed sacrifice and sustains those who approach God through Him.

To 'fill all things' means that Christ's victorious rule and life-giving presence extend throughout the sphere God has placed under Him. The church, as His body, participates in displaying that fullness. When its members use His gifts in truth and love, the reign of the ascended Christ becomes visible within the world.

The movement from descent to ascent also provides the pattern for Christian service. True exaltation came through self-giving obedience, not self-promotion. Gifts from the enthroned Christ are therefore to be exercised in the likeness of the One who humbled Himself before He was highly exalted.

wordNotes.term: fill all things — πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα (plērōsē ta panta)
wordNotes.explanation: The expression describes Christ exercising His sovereign presence and bringing God's purpose to completion throughout creation. It does not merge Christ with creation or teach pantheism.

verses.bibleText: And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The ascended Christ gives not only abilities but gifted people to His church. Their value lies in the service for which He appoints them, not in personal rank. All five ministries are connected with communicating, establishing, guarding, or applying the gospel.

Apostles were commissioned messengers with a foundational role in the church's beginning. Those directly connected with the risen Christ bore authoritative witness to His life, death, and resurrection and carried the gospel across decisive boundaries. Their foundational testimony remains in the apostolic Scriptures and cannot be replaced by later claims of equal authority.

New Testament prophets spoke messages given by the Spirit for edification, warning, guidance, and encouragement. Together with the apostles they participated in laying the church's foundation. That historical foundation is not repeatedly laid, yet the verse does not limit the Spirit's freedom to guide His people or bestow prophetic witness according to His will. Every later claim must be tested by Scripture, must exalt Christ, and must never introduce another gospel or supersede the biblical canon.

Evangelists carry the good news into places and among people who need to hear it. Philip illustrates the work through his proclamation of Christ beyond familiar boundaries, while Timothy is urged to do the work of an evangelist as part of his ministry.

Pastors are shepherds under the chief Shepherd. Their task includes feeding, protecting, guiding, seeking the straying, and caring for the vulnerable. The shepherd image forbids authoritarian control: Christ's flock belongs to Christ. Teachers preserve and explain the apostolic truth so that believers can distinguish the gospel from attractive error. Pastoral care without truth becomes directionless, while teaching without shepherd-like love can become cold or oppressive.

These ministries overlap, but none makes the rest of the church passive. Christ gives leaders so that every saint may be equipped to serve. Their success is measured not by how indispensable they become but by whether the body grows into mature dependence upon Christ.

wordNotes.term: pastors and teachers — ποιμένας καὶ διδασκάλους (poimenas kai didaskalous)
wordNotes.explanation: Pastors are shepherds who care for and guide the flock; teachers instruct the church in revealed truth. The Greek links the two functions closely, though it does not require that every teacher be a pastor.

verses.bibleText: For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Christ gives the ministries of verse 11 for the equipping of the saints. The KJV punctuation can sound as though church leaders alone perform the work of ministry and the building of the body. The flow of the Greek more naturally presents a sequence: gifted leaders equip the saints; the saints perform service; through that service the body of Christ is built up.

'Saints' means all who have been set apart in Christ, not an exceptional class of unusually holy Christians. Every believer is both a recipient of ministry and a participant in ministry. Leaders are not spiritual performers serving an audience. They train, nourish, and prepare the whole congregation to exercise the grace Christ has distributed to each member.

Perfecting means fitting people for useful service. Instruction in Scripture, development of character, correction of error, prayer, mentoring, and practical opportunities all belong to this preparation. The term does not promise instant perfection or self-sufficient holiness. Believers remain dependent upon grace while being genuinely transformed and made increasingly useful.

The goal is the 'edifying,' or building up, of Christ's body. Paul combines architectural and organic imagery. The church is God's dwelling under construction and Christ's living body growing toward maturity. Numerical increase may be part of that growth, but the emphasis lies on strength, truth, unity, love, and Christlike character.

Ministry therefore cannot be reduced to platform activity. Teaching children, visiting the sick, sharing the gospel, helping the poor, restoring the fallen, offering wise counsel, interceding, organizing service, and using one's occupation for God's glory can all contribute to the body's growth. The ascended Christ equips His entire people for a shared work.

wordNotes.explanation: The noun means equipping, preparing, or fitting for service. It concerns bringing believers into useful readiness, not claiming that they have already reached absolute sinlessness.
The word means service. Here the work of ministry belongs to the saints generally, not to a professional religious class alone.

verses.bibleText: Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The building work continues toward a shared destination: 'till we all come.' No part of Christ's body is meant to mature in isolation or at the expense of another. The whole church is moving toward unity of faith, fuller knowledge of the Son, and corporate likeness to Christ.

The unity of the faith is more than friendly agreement. It includes common commitment to the apostolic gospel. Verse 14's warning about false doctrine shows that doctrinal content matters. Yet unity is not produced by winning arguments alone. It grows as believers know the Son of God—not merely as a subject of study but as the living Lord whose character reshapes their relationships.

The 'perfect man' is the mature person in contrast with the children of the next verse. The singular recalls the 'one new man' Christ created from divided peoples. Paul is describing corporate maturity: the reconciled humanity in Christ growing into what its Head intends it to be. Individual growth is indispensable, but it occurs within the body.

The measure is nothing less than the stature of Christ's fullness. Human tradition, institutional success, or comparison with other believers cannot serve as the final standard. Christ Himself is the pattern and goal. His truth, love, holiness, humility, courage, and self-giving service define maturity.

This language should not be turned into perfectionism. Paul includes himself among those who have not yet arrived, and elsewhere he acknowledges continued growth. Grace produces real victory over sin and genuine Christlike development, but no believer becomes independent of Christ or beyond the need of mercy. The complete manifestation of what God's children will be awaits Christ's appearing, the resurrection, and their transformation into His likeness.

Until then, the church must neither excuse stagnation nor claim completion. It grows toward the fullness already present in its Head, confident that the One who calls and equips His people will finish His work.

wordNotes.explanation: The expression means a mature adult. The singular primarily pictures the whole church growing as one new humanity rather than isolated individuals attaining independent perfection.

wordNotes.term: knowledge of the Son of God — ἐπίγνωσις τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ (epignōsis tou huiou tou theou)
wordNotes.explanation: This knowledge includes accurate recognition of who Christ is and a deepening relational participation in His life. It is neither bare information nor secret knowledge for an elite.

verses.bibleText: That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Maturity protects the church from remaining spiritually childlike. Children possess valuable openness and dependence, but they also lack developed judgment. Paul focuses on that vulnerability. Without grounding in the gospel, believers can be driven by whatever teaching is newest, most dramatic, or most confidently presented.

The maritime imagery is forceful. A small vessel without stability is lifted by waves and redirected by every changing wind. The danger is not honest inquiry or continued learning. Mature faith remains teachable. Instability appears when convictions are governed by personalities, trends, fear, or excitement rather than Scripture and the knowledge of Christ.

Some falsehood arises from confusion; the language here includes deliberate manipulation. The 'sleight' of men suggests cheating, while cunning craftiness describes calculated skill used in the service of error. Religious deception often mixes truth with distortion, appeals to secret insight, produces dependence upon a teacher, or promises spiritual advantage through methods Scripture has not given.

The remedy is not suspicion of every teacher or withdrawal into private interpretation. Christ has given teachers to the body precisely so believers may learn together. Claims must be tested by the apostolic gospel, the whole counsel of Scripture, the character of Jesus, and the fruit produced in life. Teaching that diminishes Christ's deity, weakens His saving sufficiency, excuses sin, abolishes God's moral will, or exalts human authority above Scripture cannot lead the body to its Head.

Doctrinal stability is relational as well as intellectual. Believers become less vulnerable as they know Christ, participate in a truthful community, and exercise their own gifts. A mature church neither chases every wind nor fears careful reexamination. It remains firmly anchored while growing in understanding.

wordNotes.term: sleight of men — κυβεία τῶν ἀνθρώπων (kybeia tōn anthrōpōn)
wordNotes.explanation: Kybeia is associated with dice-playing and came to suggest trickery or cheating. The image exposes teaching shaped to manipulate hearers rather than communicate truth.
The word denotes unscrupulous cleverness. Intelligence becomes spiritually dangerous when used to construct persuasive systems of error.

verses.bibleText: But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
In place of manipulation and instability, believers are to practice the truth in love. The Greek expression is broader than verbal accuracy. It describes a life aligned with the truth of the gospel—confessing it, teaching it, embodying it, and dealing truthfully with others.

Truth and love must remain joined. Truth without love can become a weapon for self-exaltation, humiliating the weak while congratulating the speaker for courage. Love without truth becomes sentiment that leaves people within destructive error. Christ embodies both. His grace never required Him to call evil good, and His truth was never separated from His saving purpose.

The goal is growth 'into him.' Christian maturity is not merely the development of stronger opinions or greater independence. Every area of the body is to come increasingly under Christ's direction. Thought, worship, relationships, work, sexuality, speech, use of possessions, and response to conflict all belong to His lordship.

Christ is the Head, the source of the body's life and the authority who directs it. Leaders cannot take His place, and individual members cannot detach themselves from Him while claiming spiritual maturity. Growth is measured by deeper conformity to the One who gave Himself for the church.

Love determines not whether truth will be spoken but why, when, and how. It asks what will genuinely build another person, chooses words fitted to the need, and remains willing to listen. A church that truths in love becomes both doctrinally stable and relationally alive.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb can include speaking, holding, and living according to the truth. It calls for a truthful way of life rather than correct words alone.

verses.bibleText: From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
All growth begins 'from' Christ. The church does not build itself through autonomous human energy. Its life, direction, gifts, and power flow from the Head. Yet Christ ordinarily produces growth through the active participation of the body's members.

The body is fitly joined and held together. Different parts are not randomly collected but placed in relationships of mutual dependence. No member possesses every gift, and no member can say to another, 'I have no need of thee.' A healthy church therefore resists both individualism and domination. Members retain distinct functions while sharing one life.

Every supporting connection supplies something needed. Teaching, encouragement, correction, compassion, material assistance, prayer, hospitality, administration, evangelism, and quiet faithfulness may all become channels through which Christ nourishes His people. The body weakens when members consume without serving or when leaders prevent others from exercising their gifts.

Each part works 'according to the measure' assigned to it. Faithfulness does not require carrying another person's calling or attempting every task. It means receiving one's portion from Christ and employing it for the common good. A seemingly small contribution may be essential to the body's health.

The body makes increase toward the edifying of itself in love. This is not self-generated growth, because the sentence begins with Christ. The church builds itself only as Christ supplies and coordinates its members. Love is the environment and purpose of the entire process. Gifts exercised without love may attract attention but do not produce the growth Paul envisions.

The mature church is therefore neither a crowd gathered around a few gifted personalities nor a collection of private Christians. It is a living body in which every member remains connected to Christ and contributes to the welfare of the whole.

wordNotes.term: fitly joined together and compacted — συναρμολογούμενον καὶ συμβιβαζόμενον (synarmologoumenon kai symbibazomenon)
wordNotes.explanation: The terms describe parts being carefully joined and held together. The body's unity is ordered and interdependent rather than accidental.
The phrase refers to every supporting connection through which the body receives what it needs. It emphasizes relationships and channels of mutual supply.

verses.bibleText: This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that ye henceforth walk not as other Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their mind,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
A second solemn appeal begins with language resembling verse 1. Paul both says and testifies 'in the Lord,' placing the instruction under Christ's authority. The worthy walk now receives a negative definition: believers must no longer live according to the pattern of the unbelieving world from which they have been called.

The readers remain Gentiles ethnically, but their deepest identity has changed. 'Other Gentiles' here describes people whose lives remain apart from Christ. Paul is not declaring that every non-Christian displays every vice to the same degree. Scripture recognizes acts of civic justice and conscience among the nations. His concern is the underlying orientation of a life estranged from the Creator.

The problem begins in the mind. Futility is not absence of intelligence, education, art, or practical skill. Ephesus possessed impressive culture, commerce, religion, and learning. Yet thought that excludes the true God loses its final reference point. It may accomplish immediate goals while failing to answer what human life is for or to lead people into reconciliation with their Maker.

Idolatry and futility reinforce one another. When created things receive the trust and allegiance due to God, human beings become shaped by objects incapable of giving life. Desire becomes disordered, moral reasoning darkens, and conduct follows.

Conversion therefore involves a transformed way of thinking as well as changed religious affiliation. The church must not merely replace pagan ceremonies with Christian ceremonies while retaining ambition, greed, sensuality, and pride. To learn Christ is to receive a new center from which the whole life is understood and lived.

wordNotes.term: vanity of their mind — ματαιότης τοῦ νοός (mataiotēs tou noos)
wordNotes.explanation: Mataiotēs conveys futility, emptiness, aimlessness, and failure to reach the proper goal. A mind alienated from God cannot provide a sound foundation for life.

verses.bibleText: Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Futile thinking is accompanied by darkened understanding. Darkness here is moral and spiritual: reality is interpreted without the light that comes from God's self-revelation. The condition affects reason, affections, conscience, and judgment together.

The result is alienation from 'the life of God.' God alone possesses life in Himself and gives life to His creatures. Human beings do not carry an independent, naturally indestructible life that can flourish apart from Him. Separation from the Source of life leads toward corruption and death. Eternal life is God's gift in His Son, not an inherent possession of the soul.

Paul traces this alienation to ignorance and hardness of heart. The ignorance is real, but it is not always morally innocent. Repeated refusal of light produces insensitivity. The heart becomes calloused, and the person loses responsiveness to truth once recognized. Conversely, hardness also deepens ignorance, because a will resistant to God finds reasons not to understand Him.

The diagnosis leaves no room for intellectual pride among believers. They were not delivered because they were naturally clearer thinkers or morally superior. God enlightened the eyes of their hearts, brought them near by Christ's blood, and made them alive by grace. Knowledge of God remains a gift that should produce humility.

The verse also warns against treating spiritual dullness as a harmless condition. Rejected truth can gradually become harder to hear. The Spirit renews understanding through Scripture, prayer, obedience, and fellowship, but believers must remain responsive. Light received is meant to be followed.

wordNotes.term: alienated from the life of God — ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ θεοῦ (apēllotriōmenoi tēs zōēs tou theou)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase describes estrangement from the life God gives and sustains. It does not mean that creatures share God's self-existent essence.

wordNotes.term: blindness of their heart — πώρωσις τῆς καρδίας (pōrōsis tēs kardias)
wordNotes.explanation: The Greek word denotes hardness, callousness, or loss of sensitivity. The condition involves moral resistance and spiritual dullness, not merely lack of information.

verses.bibleText: Who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The downward movement reaches conduct. When the heart becomes insensitive to God, restraint is increasingly experienced as an obstacle rather than protection. People may then hand themselves over to desires that promise freedom but produce deeper slavery.

'Past feeling' suggests callousness—the loss of moral pain that once warned against evil. It may also include despair. When life appears aimless and hope disappears, reckless pleasure can become an attempted escape. Numbness and self-indulgence are therefore not far apart.

They 'gave themselves over.' Human responsibility remains present. Evil influences, distorted culture, and spiritual powers are real, but people also surrender their choices to destructive desire. The language parallels the tragedy in Romans 1, where rejection of God results in being given over to the path chosen.

Lasciviousness is shameless disregard of moral boundaries, especially in sexual conduct. 'Greediness' describes an appetite that continually demands more. Sin cannot satisfy the hunger it stimulates. What begins as the pursuit of pleasure becomes the laboring, or working, of uncleanness.

Paul's purpose is not to cultivate contempt for unbelievers. He has already reminded the Ephesians that they formerly walked in the same world of disobedience. The description should awaken gratitude, vigilance, and compassion. Grace rescues people from this condition without pretending it is harmless.

The church must also guard against reproducing the same pattern under religious language. Whenever desire is treated as self-validating, other people become objects, and moral limits are dismissed as oppression, the old humanity is reasserting itself. Life in Christ restores sensitivity, hope, self-control, and respect for bodies created by God.

wordNotes.explanation: The word can describe becoming callous or losing moral sensitivity; it may also carry the sense of despairing abandonment. Both ideas fit a life emptied of its true goal in God.
The term denotes shameless, unrestrained conduct, often involving sexual immorality and defiant pursuit of pleasure without regard for God's will or another person's good.

verses.bibleText: But ye have not so learned Christ;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The contrast is abrupt and emphatic: 'But ye have not so learned Christ.' Christianity is not the pagan way of life with a new religious label. Nothing in the Christ they received teaches callousness, greed, impurity, or surrender to deceitful desire.

Paul does not merely say that they learned Christian rules. They 'learned Christ.' The gospel communicates truths about His identity and work, yet those truths bring believers into fellowship with a living Person. Christ is the message proclaimed, the Lord obeyed, the pattern followed, and the life dwelling within His people.

This makes Christian ethics inseparable from Christology. Conduct is not transformed by an arbitrary code added after salvation. The One who saves also defines the new life. His humility opposes pride, His purity opposes uncleanness, His truth opposes deceit, and His self-giving love opposes greed.

Learning Christ remains a continuing vocation. Conversion begins the relationship but does not exhaust its depths. Through Scripture, prayer, obedience, and life in the body, believers come to know Him more fully. Knowledge that leaves conduct unchanged has not yet accomplished the learning Paul describes.

wordNotes.term: learned Christ — ἐμάθετε τὸν Χριστόν (emathete ton Christon)
wordNotes.explanation: The unusual expression presents Christ Himself as the content and living center of Christian learning. Believers learn about Him by entering a relationship of faith and discipleship with Him.

verses.bibleText: If so be that ye have heard him, and have been taught by him, as the truth is in Jesus:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The expression 'if so be' is best heard as an assumption rather than a taunt. Paul expects that his readers have truly heard Christ and been taught by Him. Most had not listened to Jesus during His earthly ministry, but the apostolic gospel brought the living Lord's message to them. When Christ is faithfully preached, hearers are summoned by Christ Himself.

They were taught 'by him,' or more literally, 'in him.' Christian instruction takes place within the relationship created by union with Christ. Information is indispensable, but the teaching is not detached from worship, trust, and obedience.

The phrase 'truth is in Jesus' gives special attention to the historical Jesus. The ethics of the church cannot be built upon an abstract Christ shaped by imagination. The real Jesus of Nazareth—incarnate Son, obedient servant, teacher, crucified Savior, risen Lord—is the measure of Christian truth.

His life exposes the false division between doctrine and conduct. Truth includes what He taught and what He embodied. A message may use Christian vocabulary yet be false if it contradicts His character, minimizes His saving work, or permits a life opposed to His holiness.

Believers therefore test spiritual claims by the apostolic witness to Jesus. Private revelation, cultural fashion, and religious tradition remain subordinate. Truth is not whatever produces a strong experience; it is centered in the One who is Himself the way, the truth, and the life.

wordNotes.term: the truth is in Jesus — ἀλήθεια ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ (alētheia en tō Iēsou)
wordNotes.explanation: Christian truth is embodied and revealed in the historical Jesus—His teaching, character, saving work, death, resurrection, and present lordship.

verses.bibleText: That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Learning Christ includes putting off the old man. Paul uses the image of removing clothing to describe a decisive change of identity and the continuing rejection of conduct belonging to the former life.

The old man is not the material body, as though physical existence were inherently evil. It is the old humanity under sin—the pattern of thought, desire, and action described in verses 17–19. In union with Christ, that former identity has received its judgment at the cross. Believers are therefore called to live consistently with what God has done, removing the habits that still seek expression.

The language holds together an accomplished change and an ongoing responsibility. Conversion is more than gradual moral improvement: the believer has passed from the old realm into the new. Yet remnants of former behavior do not disappear without resistance, repentance, and daily dependence upon the Spirit. Grace neither leaves the old life untouched nor makes human choices irrelevant.

The old humanity is 'corrupt according to the deceitful lusts.' Desire becomes deceptive when it promises life apart from God's will. Greed promises security, lust promises intimacy, revenge promises relief, and pride promises significance. Each offers what it cannot finally give. The process is one of continuing corruption: the more deceitful desire governs, the more the person disintegrates morally and relationally.

Putting off the old man means refusing those lies because Christ has revealed a better reality. It includes confession, practical separation from occasions of sin, restitution where possible, renewed patterns, and reliance upon divine power. The command is not an attempt to earn a new identity. It is the obedient expression of the new identity received by grace.

wordNotes.term: the old man — ὁ παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος (ho palaios anthrōpos)
wordNotes.explanation: The old man is the former humanity shaped by sin, alienation, and the old manner of life. It is not the physical body itself.

wordNotes.term: deceitful lusts — ἐπιθυμίαι τῆς ἀπάτης (epithymiai tēs apatēs)
wordNotes.explanation: These are desires generated or governed by deceit. They promise fulfillment while progressively corrupting the person who follows them.

verses.bibleText: And be renewed in the spirit of your mind;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Between putting off the old humanity and putting on the new stands continual renewal. External behavior changes sustainably when the inward orientation of the mind is being transformed.

Renewal involves more than acquiring religious information. The old way of life also possessed beliefs, assumptions, memories, and desires. The Spirit brings these under the truth of Christ, teaching believers to see God, themselves, other people, possessions, suffering, sexuality, and the future differently.

The passive form indicates that renewal is God's work. Human effort cannot recreate the inner person. Yet passivity is not spiritual indifference. Believers receive the Word, pray, obey known truth, reject deceptive thoughts, participate in fellowship, and set their minds upon what reflects Christ. Through these means the Spirit performs the transformation.

The renewal is ongoing. Conversion gives a new allegiance and life, but the mind continues to require cleansing and reformation. Old patterns can reappear, cultural assumptions can remain unexamined, and truth already confessed may need deeper application.

Sanctification therefore combines dependence and responsibility. The believer neither reforms himself without grace nor waits for holiness while resisting the Spirit's means. God renews the mind so that obedience becomes increasingly intelligent, willing, and rooted in love.

wordNotes.explanation: The present passive form describes continuing renewal received from God. Believers actively yield to a transformation they cannot produce independently.

wordNotes.term: the spirit of your mind — τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν (to pneuma tou noos hymōn)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase points to the deepest inward orientation of thought and perception. The Holy Spirit is the divine agent who accomplishes this inner renewal.

verses.bibleText: And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The positive counterpart to removing the old garment is putting on the new man. Salvation restores what sin has defaced. The language echoes humanity's creation in God's image and Ephesians 2, where believers are God's workmanship and divided peoples are created into one new humanity in Christ.

The new man is 'created.' Moral renewal is therefore an act of divine grace, not a human achievement built from the remains of the old life. God does not merely improve the sinner's public appearance. He creates a new relationship, allegiance, and capacity through union with Christ and the indwelling Spirit.

This new creation appears in 'righteousness and true holiness.' Righteousness concerns life aligned with God's right order, while holiness reflects consecration to His character and will. The two together describe a life that increasingly resembles its Creator.

Grace does not erase moral distinctions or abolish God's righteous law. The new covenant places God's will within the heart, where the Spirit produces what external command alone could never accomplish. The moral law cannot justify sinners, but the Christ who justifies also restores them to loving obedience. The righteousness of the law is fulfilled in those who walk according to the Spirit, not as the price of acceptance but as its fruit.

'Putting on' expresses an identity already bestowed and a life that must be consciously lived. Holiness is neither a costume for religious occasions nor instant sinless independence. It is the continuing embodiment of the truth found in Jesus.

The corporate dimension must remain visible. The new man is not merely a collection of improved individuals. It is the reconciled humanity Christ created from former enemies. Righteousness and holiness therefore include how believers cross social boundaries, speak truth, share possessions, forgive, and preserve the unity of the body.

wordNotes.term: the new man — ὁ καινὸς ἄνθρωπος (ho kainos anthrōpos)
wordNotes.explanation: The expression describes the qualitatively new humanity created in Christ. It applies to the renewed believer and, in Ephesians, to the reconciled corporate people Christ has made one.

wordNotes.term: true holiness — ὁσιότης τῆς ἀληθείας (hosiotēs tēs alētheias)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase denotes holiness arising from and governed by the truth, in contrast with the deceptive desires that corrupt the old humanity.

verses.bibleText: Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The new creation becomes visible in ordinary speech. Falsehood belongs to the old man because that old order is governed by deceitful desires. Those who have learned the truth in Jesus must remove lying as they would remove a corrupted garment.

The command to speak truth echoes Zechariah's instruction to the restored people of God. Truthfulness is part of life within the renewed covenant community. It includes refusing direct lies, misleading impressions, dishonest silence, manipulated statistics, false accusations, broken promises, and theological distortions.

The reason is distinctly communal: 'we are members one of another.' A lie never remains private within a body. It damages trust, misdirects decisions, and injures a person whose welfare is connected with one's own. Deceiving another member is like one part of the body sending false information to another.

Truthfulness does not require disclosing every private fact to every person, nor does it justify cruel or reckless speech. Verse 15 has already joined truth with love. Wisdom considers confidentiality, safety, timing, and the hearer's need. Yet love cannot be used as a pretext for deception.

A truthful church becomes a place where confession, correction, reconciliation, and sound teaching are possible. Where appearances must always be maintained, sin remains hidden and people suffer alone. Speaking truth as fellow members creates the conditions in which grace can heal.

wordNotes.term: putting away lying — ἀποθέμενοι τὸ ψεῦδος (apothemenoi to pseudos)
wordNotes.explanation: The wording continues the clothing image: falsehood belongs to the discarded old humanity and must no longer characterize the believer.

verses.bibleText: Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul quotes the Greek form of Psalm 4:4: 'Be ye angry, and sin not.' The wording has been understood either as permission for righteous anger or as a practical concession: when anger arises, do not allow it to become sin. The following commands place the emphasis on restraint, prompt resolution, and refusal to nourish resentment.

Anger is not automatically identical with sin. God is angered by evil, and Jesus grieved with anger at hardheartedness. Moral indifference toward cruelty and injustice is not a Christian virtue. Yet divine anger is perfectly holy, while human anger is easily mixed with wounded pride, prejudice, exaggeration, or desire for revenge.

Anger becomes sinful when it dehumanizes, seeks injury, distorts truth, refuses correction, or takes pleasure in another's downfall. It can also become sin through silence when resentment is stored and repeatedly rehearsed. The command calls for honest recognition of the emotion without surrendering judgment and conduct to it.

The setting of the sun gives proverbial urgency. Paul is not establishing a mechanical rule that every complex dispute must be fully settled before a literal sunset. Some situations require time, mediation, safety planning, or legal action. His warning is against allowing anger to settle into a cherished condition. Delay gives imagination time to deepen accusation and prepare retaliation.

Prompt reconciliation does not mean suppressing truth or returning an abused person to danger. It means refusing malice, seeking a righteous resolution where possible, and entrusting final vengeance to God. Anger must be brought under Christ's lordship quickly, because within the one body its unchecked power can destroy both the angry person and the community.

wordNotes.term: be ye angry, and sin not — ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε (orgizesthe kai mē hamartanete)
wordNotes.explanation: The words reproduce Psalm 4:4 in the Greek Old Testament. They recognize anger as a dangerous reality and command that it not be allowed to develop into sinful thought, speech, or action.
The noun can describe provocation, intense irritation, or festering anger. The context emphasizes anger allowed to remain unresolved and grow.

verses.bibleText: Neither give place to the devil.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Unresolved anger is not merely an emotional problem; it creates an opening for the devil. The adversary seeks to divide what Christ has reconciled, corrupt truthful speech, and turn legitimate grievances into bitterness, slander, and revenge.

Giving place does not mean that every angry feeling amounts to demonic possession. It means that cherished anger supplies an opportunity for satanic purposes. Suspicion grows, motives are misrepresented, parties form, and the unity of the Spirit is wounded.

Resistance begins with refusing the foothold. Confession, prayer, truthful conversation, wise mediation, forgiveness, and appropriate boundaries close the space in which resentment flourishes. The struggle is spiritual, but its battlefield includes ordinary decisions about words, memories, and relationships.

The devil's schemes are real, yet the verse gives him no excuse for human sin. Believers are commanded not to provide the opportunity. Christ has already defeated the hostile powers, and those united to Him can resist rather than yield.

wordNotes.explanation: The idiom means giving an opportunity, room, or foothold. Unresolved sin creates circumstances the devil can exploit.

verses.bibleText: Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The gospel transforms more than the thief's outward act. Paul traces a complete movement from taking, to honest labor, to generous sharing. The former thief does not merely stop causing harm; his hands become instruments of good.

The command affirms the continuing moral force of 'Thou shalt not steal.' Grace does not make property, honesty, or justice irrelevant. It frees the sinner from condemnation and creates a life that increasingly reflects God's righteousness. Obedience is the fruit of new creation, never the means by which pardon is earned.

Manual work receives honor. In a culture where difficult physical labor was often associated with lower status, Paul treats work with one's own hands as honorable service. The work must be 'the thing which is good'—honest and beneficial rather than exploitative or destructive.

The purpose reaches beyond self-support: 'that he may have to give to him that needeth.' Christian labor is not directed solely toward private accumulation. Earnings provide for legitimate responsibilities and also create the capacity to assist the vulnerable. The person who once reduced another's resources now contributes to another's welfare.

Generosity does not erase prudence or encourage dependency without discernment. It does reveal a transformed relationship to possessions. The new humanity understands property as a stewardship under God. Work, saving, spending, and giving are all brought beneath Christ's lordship.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes strenuous, tiring work. Conversion redirects the hands from secretly taking what belongs to another toward honest, productive, and generous service.

verses.bibleText: Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Speech is evaluated not only by whether it is factually correct but by what it produces. Rotten communication includes obscenity, deception, slander, ridicule, manipulative teaching, malicious gossip, and words that needlessly corrode another person's dignity or faith.

The image is stronger than impoliteness. Rotten food spreads decay and cannot nourish. In the same way, destructive speech can contaminate a community, remain in memory long after it is spoken, and weaken people who needed strength.

The positive alternative is speech 'good to the use of edifying.' Words should be fitted to the need. The same statement may help in one setting and harm in another because timing, tone, relationship, and spiritual condition differ. Wisdom asks what truth the hearer needs and how it can be communicated faithfully and lovingly.

To 'minister grace' does not mean that human speech conveys saving merit or replaces the Spirit. It means that words can become instruments through which God's favor strengthens, corrects, comforts, and equips another person. Encouragement may restore courage; correction may rescue from error; instruction may prepare someone for ministry; confession may reopen fellowship.

Edifying speech is not perpetual pleasantness. Jesus sometimes spoke severe words, and loving correction can be painful. The distinction lies in purpose and spirit. Rotten speech uses truth to injure or falsehood to control. Gracious speech serves God's redemptive purpose in the hearer.

Because the church builds itself in love, every conversation participates either in construction or demolition. The tongue is therefore part of Christian ministry.

wordNotes.explanation: Sapros literally describes something rotten, decayed, diseased, or useless. Applied to speech, it includes words that corrupt, deceive, degrade, or contribute nothing beneficial.
The word means building up. Speech should strengthen the hearer and contribute to the maturity of Christ's body according to the actual need.

verses.bibleText: And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The warning against harmful speech leads into a command concerning the Holy Spirit. Words that corrupt the body grieve the Spirit who created its unity and dwells within it. Sin against fellow members is never merely horizontal, because the community is God's temple.

The Spirit can be grieved. He is not an impersonal energy that believers use for religious power. He knows, wills, teaches, sanctifies, and responds personally to rebellion. The wording recalls Isaiah's account of Israel: God redeemed His people, carried them, and gave them His Spirit, yet they rebelled and grieved Him. Privilege did not make disobedience insignificant.

Believers have been sealed by the Spirit. A seal could identify ownership, authenticate what was genuine, and protect what belonged to an authority. The Spirit's presence marks God's people as His own and serves as the earnest, or pledge, of the inheritance.

The seal gives assurance without encouraging presumption. It rests upon God's faithfulness and the sufficiency of Christ, not upon human merit. Yet the command not to grieve the Spirit shows that relationship with Him can be resisted. The seal does not remove human freedom, make apostasy impossible by definition, or turn persistent rebellion into a harmless matter. Assurance flourishes as believers continue trusting Christ and yielding to the Spirit who witnesses to Him.

The seal points forward to 'the day of redemption.' Redemption has already been secured by Christ's blood, but its full effect is future. At Christ's return the dead in Him will be raised, the living faithful transformed, and the body delivered from corruption. The Christian hope is therefore not final existence as a conscious disembodied soul but completed salvation through resurrection and immortality bestowed by God.

Every present prompting of the Spirit belongs to that future purpose. He is preparing a people for the day of redemption. To cherish bitterness, falsehood, impurity, or destructive speech is to resist the One shaping believers for the kingdom they hope to inherit.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to cause sorrow or distress. Its use confirms that the Holy Spirit is a personal divine presence who can be resisted, not merely an impersonal force.

wordNotes.term: sealed unto the day of redemption — ἐσφραγίσθητε εἰς ἡμέραν ἀπολυτρώσεως (esphragisthēte eis hēmeran apolytrōseōs)
wordNotes.explanation: The Spirit's seal marks believers as belonging to God and serves as the pledge of their future deliverance. The day of redemption includes the completion of salvation at Christ's return and the redemption of the body.

verses.bibleText: Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul gathers several forms of hostile disposition and speech into one command: they must be removed. The terms need not represent a fixed sequence, though they often reinforce one another. Bitterness stores injury; wrath erupts; anger settles into hostility; clamour raises its voice; evil speaking attacks another's reputation; malice supplies the vicious intention beneath them all.

The command reaches deeper than outward politeness. A person may stop shouting while continuing to rehearse accusations inwardly. The new humanity requires the removal of the disposition that desires another's humiliation or harm.

'All' is comprehensive. Believers are not invited to preserve a respectable portion of resentment because the original wrong was real. Justice and forgiveness are not enemies, but revenge and Christlike love are. Proper accountability may continue, consequences may remain, and reconciliation may require repentance and safety. What must disappear is the malice that seeks evil for the offender.

Putting away bitterness does not require an abused person to conceal wrongdoing, abandon lawful protection, or restore unsafe access. Truthful reporting and wise boundaries can serve justice and prevent further harm. The verse addresses the spirit in which these actions are taken: without slander, uncontrolled rage, or personal vengeance.

The church cannot preserve the unity of the Spirit while normalizing hostile speech. The old humanity forms factions through accusation; the new humanity makes room for truth, justice, repentance, and grace.

wordNotes.explanation: Bitterness is a sharp, resentful disposition that preserves injury and interprets others through accumulated grievance.

wordNotes.term: clamour and evil speaking — κραυγὴ καὶ βλασφημία (kraugē kai blasphēmia)
wordNotes.explanation: Clamour is angry shouting or public outcry; evil speaking includes abusive speech, insult, and slander that damages another person's name.

verses.bibleText: And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The vices of verse 31 are not merely suppressed; they are replaced. Kindness takes the place of malice, tenderheartedness replaces callousness, and forgiveness answers resentment. Christian transformation is positive creation, not moral emptiness.

Kindness reflects the undeserved kindness God displayed when He made sinners alive with Christ. It seeks another person's genuine good in concrete ways. Tenderheartedness is deep responsiveness to another's weakness, sorrow, and need. The heart once hardened through alienation is softened by the mercy it has received.

Believers are to forgive one another 'even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.' The underlying sense is that God has forgiven in Christ. Forgiveness rests upon Christ's atoning self-gift, not upon God's indifference to sin. At the cross, justice and mercy meet in the once-for-all sacrifice of the Son. Nothing in human forgiveness supplements that sacrifice or earns divine pardon.

The order is essential. Christians do not forgive so that God may become willing to forgive them. They forgive because God has already acted graciously toward them in Christ. The forgiven debtor is called to extend the grace by which he lives.

Forgiveness does not mean declaring evil unreal, removing every consequence, or immediately restoring trust. Trust may need to be rebuilt, civil justice may be necessary, and safety may require distance. Forgiveness releases personal vengeance, refuses to define the offender solely by the wrong, and remains open to the redemptive work of God.

The chapter that began with the call to walk worthy ends at the cross-shaped center of that walk. Unity, ministry, truth, holiness, speech, work, and reconciliation all flow from grace. The church becomes visibly new when people who have been forgiven by God learn to treat one another according to the same mercy.

wordNotes.explanation: The word describes deep compassion arising from the inward person. It is the opposite of the callousness described in verse 18.
The verb is related to grace and means freely granting favor or forgiveness. Christian forgiveness arises from grace already received in Christ.
